content.title: Official Blind Review #3
content.review:
Summary:
This paper proposes to examine robustness against more unforeseen attacks (than Lp attacks) such as Elastic, Fog and Snow etc. The Unforeseen Attack Robustness (UAT) evaluation metric is further proposed to produce a consistent score over a range of test attacks and perturbations sizes. They also demonstrate the overfitting issue of joint adversarial training on 2 different norms of attacks.

--------------
My concerns:
1. It is hard to tell which type of robustness is evaluating in this paper: adversarial or common corruptions? Adversarial robustness often refer to robustness to small imperceptible adversarial perturbations, however, many of the perturbations illustrated in this paper are neither small nor imperceptible. I would expect none of existing models can survive any of those large perturbations. On the other hand, the new attacks proposed in this paper are basically common corruptions, which has been comprehensively studied in [1] on 15 types of corruptions including the proposed Elastic, fog and snow. I don't think adversarially perturb those common corruptions can contribute more for robustness evaluation. There are also other corruptions such as translations and rotations [2].

2. The real contribution of this paper is not clear to me. What is the focus of this paper: the robustness of different DNNs, training strategies or defense techniques? Why only one type of defense (eg. adversarial training) was considered (why not a few latest works in adversarial training: [3][4])? My concern comes from this "one-defense" setting. Since all models are trained by one fixed defense, it is hard to draw any concrete conclusions on other defenses, or defense in general.  In the abstract, the authors claimed that "These results underscore the need to evaluate and study robustness against unforeseen distortions", which seems quite obvious. It is always beneficial to include more corruptions, but why the suggested Elastic, Fog, Snow in particular? 
So far, defense techniques still suffer from low robustness to even small perturbations (the strongest defense, adversarial training, only has 43% - 65% robustness against PGD perturbation L_{\infty} < 8/255). Then the question is, why evaluating against so many attacks is necessary and important, considering they even fail the easiest Lp corruptions?
By the way, in Table 1, why the ATA4 is 66.9, which seems too high, even higher than state-of-the-art robustness?

3. The proposed \epsilon_{min} and \epsilon_{max} calibration is a bit confusing. "The minimum distortion size \epsilon_{min} is the largest \epsilon for which the adversarial validation accuracy against an adversarially trained model is comparable to that of a model trained and evaluated on unattacked data." -- what this means, exactly? The proposed UAR score is also not clear: 1) what is the different between Acc and ATA? 2) "ATA is the best adversarial accuracy on the validation set that can be achieved by adversarially training a specific architecture" -- how this best accuracy was obtained?? 3) the validation set is also confusing, is it part of the training data held out for validation?
"To make UAR roughly comparable between distortions, we evaluate at \epsilon increasing geometrically from \epsilon_{min} to \epsilon_{max} by factors of 2 and take the subset of \epsilon whose ATA values have minimum `1-distance to the ATA values of the L1 attack at geometrically increasing " -- I have no idea what the authors are referring to here.

4. The presentation can be improved. For example, shorten the ticks used in those matrix plots (Figure 6, 7, etc). It can also benefit from a summary table somewhere about all those distortion types and sizes. It also helps if the authors can explain the \epsilon_{min}, \epsilon_{max} and UAR score with a more concrete example.

[1] Benchmarking Neural Network Robustness to Common Corruptions and Surface Variations
[2] The limitations of adversarial training and the blind-spot attack. ICLR 2019
[3] Theoretically principled trade-off between robustness and accuracy. ICML, 2019.
[4] On the Convergence and Robustness of Adversarial Training. ICML, 2019.

content.title: Reply to review part 1
content.comment:
Thank you for your comments and questions.   Specific responses are below:

1. type of robustness / focus of paper: Our contribution is studying how adversarial robustness varies over different types of distortions and providing methods for evaluating against different adversarial attacks.
    - large perturbations: The distortion sizes we use include some bringing undefended models to sub-10 accuracy with distortions which are imperceptible, minor, or weather related (see new Figure 22, Appendix).  They are chosen so that adversarially trained models have a wide range of performance (Table 1) but remain human-identifiable (Figs 1, 3, 5). 
    - adversarial distortions vs. common corruptions: As noted, several of our new attacks (JPEG, Fog, Snow) are adversarial version of common corruptions, but they can exhibit qualitatively different behaviors than common corruptions (Fig 3, randomly initialized snow is the common corruptions version).  We ran a smaller set of defenses against ImageNet-C (new Appendix F) and observed several important differences in behavior between adversarial attacks and common corruptions.  First, adversarial training against Elastic and L_{\infty} is effective against JPEG corruptions (Figure 21, Appendix), but not adversarial JPEG (Figure 6a).  Second, increasing the level of adversarial training hurts performance against common JPEG, Elastic, and Snow corruptions (Figure 21), but helps performance against the adversarial versions (Figure 12, Appendix).
    - translations and rotations: We ran some preliminary experiments using the spatial grid attack from https://arxiv.org/pdf/1712.02779.pdf, but found it to be extremely weak compared to Fog, Gabor, Snow, and especially Elastic, which it has some similarities to.
2. Why only adversarial training?: 
    - studying more distortions is “obvious”: While we agree studying adversarial robustness against different distortion types is a natural approach, almost none of the hundreds of papers on adversarial examples in the literature do not take this approach [1-6].  The ones which do most often introduce a single new attack with addressing evaluation [7-8].  Our paper is the first to take this approach in a systematic way for a large class of distortions.
    - Why is evaluation against other attacks important?: We show that increasing adversarial robustness against L_p may decrease adversarial robustness against other distortions, i.e. progress on the L_p case may not help for the general problem.
    - Our contributions focus on how attacks change with distortion type, of which many (Elastic, Fog, Snow, Gabor) are more interpretable on the larger 224x224 resolution of ImageNet. The only defense method we know of scaling to ImageNet is adversarial training (only achieved in 2018).  The proposed methods from [1, 2] such as TRADES are less well-characterized variants of adversarial training not known to scale to large full resolution datasets like ImageNet-100.  There is no clear reason to believe our results will change substantially with them, while these methods would triple our compute costs, putting the proposed experiments beyond our resources.
    - Why Elastic, Fog, and Snow?: We chose these suggestions based on their low pairwise correlation in Fig 6b to balance evaluation cost and additional information revealed by evaluation.  Of course, if compute cost is not an issue, we would advocate for evaluating against our full set of attacks.
    - Adversarial robustness numbers on L_{\infty}: What dataset/model are these numbers referring to?  Our numbers in the main text are for ResNet-50 on ImageNet-100 (a 100-class subset of ImageNet), which may explain the discrepancy.

content.title: Reply to review part 2
content.comment:
3. epsilon calibration: We have updated the text to clarify; specific answers are below:
    - \eps_min: This means that the ATA of the attack at \eps_{min} is within 3pct of the accuracy (87) of a ResNet-50 trained on clean data.
    - Acc and ATA: Acc(A, \eps, M) is the accuracy of a fixed model M against an attack A at distortion size \eps.  ATA(A, \eps) is the maximum accuracy against an attack A at distortion size \eps achieved by models adversarially trained against A with different settings.
    - ATA definition: We estimate this by taking ATA(A, \eps) = \max_k Acc(A, \eps, M_k), where M_k is adversarially trained against attack A at distortion size \eps_k, and \eps_k range from \eps_{min} to \eps_{max} in a geometric sequence with ratio 2.
    - Validation set: This is the standard ImageNet-100 test set, e.g. the subset of the ImageNet-1000 test set corresponding to the classes in ImageNet-100.
    - ATA subset: Thanks for the suggestion to give a concrete example.  We do so below and have updated the main text.  
        - When calibrating Elastic in Table 1, we start with \eps_{min} = 0.25 and \eps_{max} = 16 based on the criteria in Section 3.  We then compute the ATAs at \eps \in \{0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16\}, for a total of 7 different \eps values.  We consider size-6 subsets of those ATA values, view them as vectors of length 6 in decreasing order, and compute the \ell_1-distance between these vectors and the vector for L_{\infty} shown in the first row of Table 1.  Finally, we select the \eps values for Elastic in Table 1 as those corresponding to the size-6 subset with minimum \ell_1-distance to the vector for L_\infty. 
        - The UAR score for Elastic is computed by the formula (1) with the 6 values of \eps_k given in Table 1 and normalized by the 6 ATA values shown in Table 1.
        - The idea of this calibration is to evaluate different attacks at distortion sizes corresponding to comparable strengths.
4. Thanks for the suggestions regarding presentation, which we will incorporate into the camera-ready version.

[1] Theoretically principled trade-off between robustness and accuracy. ICML, 2019.
[2] On the Convergence and Robustness of Adversarial Training. ICML, 2019.
[3] Theoretically Principled Trade-off between Robustness and Accuracy.  ICML 2019.
[4] Certified Adversarial Robustness via Randomized Smoothing. ICML 2019.
[5] On the Convergence and Robustness of Adversarial Training. ICML 2019.
[6] Defense Against Adversarial Attacks Using Feature Scattering-based Adversarial Training. NeurIPS 2019.
[7] Spatially Transformed Adversarial Examples.  ICLR 2018.
[8] EAD: Elastic-net attacks to deep neural networks via adversarial examples.  AAAI 2018.

content.title: Official Blind Review #1
content.review_assessment:_thoroughness_in_paper: I made a quick assessment of this paper.
content.review:
The paper investigates empirically to what extent adversarial training with respect to a certain set of adversaries (e.g. Projected Gradient Descent (PGD) with a maximum l_inf perturbation of epsilon) also provides robustness against types of adversaries (e.g. PGD with different l_p norm constraints). While this problem has been studied before in terms of robustness transferability between different l_p constrained adversaries, this paper proposes a few novel attacks ("JPEG", "Fog", "Garbor", "Snow") to be included in such analysis. It shows that, while robustness from/against l_p constrained adversaries transfers relatively well, this is not the case for some of the newly proposed adversaries. It therefore proposes a framework, including a new canon of adversaries (including in particular the "Fog" attack),  for a more broad assessment of empirical robustness against a variety of adversaries.

The paper contains a lot of material that should be interesting to browse through for any researcher working the area of adversarial machine learning. The number of experiments carried out and reported on is impressive. The purpose of broadly and thoroughly assessing empirical robustness against a variety of adversarial attacks is important. While the paper makes a convincing case for the importance, some of the concrete steps that it's trying to promote still seem preliminary to me. For instance, how complete is the set of adversaries in the proposed UAR framework? In the sense: isn't it to be expected that the set of sources considered in Figure 6 (b) will have to be extended, e.g. once a new adversaries has been discovered that has low correlation with any of the known adversaries? In that sense, testing robustness against unforeseen/unknown adversaries still appears to be an open problem, unless the space of adversaries is constrained and it is established that any unknown adversary is necessarily correlated with the known ones.

On the methodological side,  the calibration of distortion sizes (p.4) was not clear to me. In 1.: what exactly means "comparable"? Does 2.a ("images which confuse humans") involve surveys / user studies? And what does it mean in 2.b: "reduce accuracy of adversarially trained models to below 25"?

content.title: Reply to review
content.comment:
Thank you for your comments and questions.   Our specific responses are below:

- How complete is the set of adversaries?
    - Our proposed set of adversaries is substantially more complete than nearly every existing paper on adversarial robustness. In fact, the majority of work we are aware of evaluates only against L_p attacks at 1-2 distortion sizes [1-4], which we show (Fig 6b, Fig 4) may be actively misleading.
- Will Fig 6b need to be updated for new attacks?
    - As new attacks are developed, they will need to be added to Fig 6b; this will also reveal how correlated they are with existing attacks.  One of our contributions is a uniform methodology for analyzing new attacks in this way.
- Testing robustness requires a constrained set of adversaries
    - We agree that it is difficult to guarantee generalization to a new adversary without some constraint on the space of possible adversaries.  Testing a defense against a specific unforeseen adversary is still non-trivial because of the difficulty of normalizing for attack strength (e.g., is a defense doing well because the attack is using settings which are too weak?); UAR provides a systematic way to account for this.  In addition, our new attacks significantly extend the set of uncorrelated attacks used for evaluation in the literature [1-4], which provides a challenging benchmark which can be used to falsify claims about such generalization.
- Methodology questions (we have updated the text to clarify)
    - What does comparable mean?: This means “within 3pct” of the clean accuracy, which is 87 (see Figure 8, Appendix)
    - Does 2.a involve surveys?: We chose the cutoff heuristically by looking at O(10) generated images.  This could certainly be extended using user surveys, but we found that results were not affect too much by the specific cutoff used.
    - What does 2.b mean? This means “reduce ATA to below 25”

[1] Theoretically Principled Trade-off between Robustness and Accuracy.  ICML 2019.
[2] Certified Adversarial Robustness via Randomized Smoothing. ICML 2019.
[3] On the Convergence and Robustness of Adversarial Training. ICML 2019.
[4] Defense Against Adversarial Attacks Using Feature Scattering-based Adversarial Training. NeurIPS 2019.

content.title: Official Blind Review #2
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I assessed the sensibility of the derivations and theory.
content.review:
This paper considers the robustness against adversarial attacks in learning of deep neural networks. Other than the usual Lp-distortions, the authors introduce novel adversarial distortions, JPEG, Fog, Gabor and Snow. Then, the authors propose the summary metric, unforeseen attack robustness (UAR), to measure the robustness against a given distortion. In experiments, the authors report UAR scores for existing and novel attacks and conclude that the existing defense against Lp attacks does not generalize to unforeseen attacks and the five attacks, L_\infty, L_1, Elastic, Fog and Snow, offer greater diversity. The joint adversarial training over these five attacks is also investigated in experiments.

The four novel distortions defined in this paper are interesting and promising in practice. However, there are little theoretical discussions in this paper and most arguments look somewhat ad-hoc.

Although the experiments are in fact extensive to some extent, since the results are only for specific datasets and models, it is difficult to tell how general the obtained observations are.

Section 5 discusses the joint adversarial training by experiments. Are there any theoretical results on joint adversarial training related to the discussion here?

content.title: Reply to review
content.comment:
Thank you for your comments and questions.  As noted, our paper is almost entirely empirical, as our goal is to provide an empirical framework for evaluating adversarial defenses.   Our specific responses are below.

- “little theoretical discussions in this paper”: Many papers at ICLR are purely on empirical machine learning [6-11] (including the ICLR 2019 Best Paper [11]), and the empirical implications of our work are substantial (namely, that almost all existing papers in adversarial examples are evaluating in an unsatisfactory way).  Are there examples of theory you feel would add to this? 
- “results are only for specific datasets and models”: Most papers on adversarial examples only consider MNIST, CIFAR-10, and (infrequently) ImageNet [1-5]. Our empirical results are on ImageNet-100 and CIFAR-10 (Section C.3), of which ImageNet-100 is substantially richer than MNIST.  Furthermore, our empirical results have similar trends between these datasets. We additionally study a significantly broader set of attack types (8 vs. at most 3) than is usually considered in the literature.
- joint training theoretical results:  Our work shows a strong negative empirical result for joint training on ImageNet-100 and reveals a new overfitting phenomenon which is not present in other work on joint training which uses smaller resolution datasets (MNIST and CIFAR-10) [12].  Our contribution is to reveal this unusual and new phenomenon; what type of theory do you feel would add to this?
- “most arguments look somewhat ad-hoc”: Are there examples we could provide more information about?

[1] Theoretically Principled Trade-off between Robustness and Accuracy.  ICML 2019.
[2] Certified Adversarial Robustness via Randomized Smoothing. ICML 2019.
[3] The Odds are Odd: A Statistical Test for Detecting Adversarial Examples. ICML 2019.
[4] Parsimonious Black-Box Adversarial Attacks via Efficient Combinatorial Optimization. ICML 2019.
[5] Training for Faster Adversarial Robustness Verification via Inducing ReLU Stability.  ICLR 2019
[6] CAMOU: Learning Physical Vehicle Camouflages to Adversarially Attack Detectors in the Wild.  ICLR 2019
[7] SPIGAN: Privileged Adversarial Learning from Simulation.  ICLR 2019
[8] A Direct Approach to Robust Deep Learning Using Adversarial Networks. ICLR 2019
[9] Adversarial Reprogramming of Neural Networks. ICLR 2019.
[10] Synthetic and Natural Noise Both Break Neural Machine Translation. ICLR 2018.
[11] The Lottery Ticket Hypothesis: Finding Sparse, Trainable Neural Networks. ICLR 2019. Best paper.
[12] Adversarial Training and Robustness for Multiple Perturbations. NeurIPS 2019
